title: Add ability to suspend threads until a signal is called

milestone.title: 4.x
milestone.description: Issues and pull requests slated for an undetermined Godot 4 release.

body:
### Problem

For GDScript users that run code on threads, it often happens they want to `await` until something happens, the continue the thread execution.

Unfortunately, signals will most likely execute on the main thread, hence this means that the code being run on the thread will continue running on the main thread by default after the signal is awaiting for resumes.

To illustrate:

```GDScript
	# Code is running on a dedicated thread
	await button.pressed
	# Now code is running on the main thread
```

In the past, it has been discussed whether `await` should be smart about this and simply suspend the thread if running on one. The problem with this is, that users may also be willing to emit the signal that will resume from the thread itself and, at the time of awaiting, there is **no way for the interpreter to know on which thread the function will be resumed**.

Additionally, suspending the thread is a very different operation than awaiting. Awaiting saves the local function stack and returns immediately, while suspending stops the whole thread until another resumes it. Mixing and matching both seems, ultimately, undesired as they are not the same.

To solve this, a new static function is added to Thread by this pull request, which suspends a thread until a signal is emitted (no matter in which other thread).

### Solution

It works like this.

```GDScript
	# Suspends a thread until a button is pressed.
	Thread.suspend( button.pressed )
```

If code must do this and can run on both the main thread or a dedicated thread, it can do as follows:

```GDScript
	# Suspends a thread until a button is pressed.
	if (Thread.is_main_thread()):
		await button.pressed
	else:
		Thread.suspend( button.pressed )
```

For this, the `Thread.is_main_thread()` function (already existing in the internal Thread object) has been exposed to the engine API.

It also similarly works with returned values:

```GDScript
	# Suspends a thread until a button is pressed.
	if (Thread.is_main_thread()):
		val = await button.pressed
	else:
		val = Thread.suspend( button.pressed )
```

### Added warning

A warning was added if you try to await on a thread and resume in another, since in most cases users don't expect this to happen. It suggest using this new function instead. The warning can be disabled in the project settings if that behavior is _really_ intended.

### FAQ

**Q**: Are you sure this can't be done with await transparently?
**A**: No, please read again. There is no way for await to know beforehand how the function will be resumed. Only the user knows.

**Q**: Does it not make more sense to have an `await_thread` or something where the user will pass the argument?
**A**: I think its better to have a dedicated utility function for this. Not only the intention is more explicit, but additionally, as this makes it non exclusive to GDScript. It can be used from other languages that work with the engine.

**Q**: Thread safety wise, isn't connecting to a signal non-thread safe? Is this not a problem?
**A**: Yes, it is up to the user to protect and make sure nothing is connecting or emitting while the thread suspends. I think signals should be made thread safe, though at some point in the future.

**Q**: What happens if you await on a method ? How do you do it with suspend?
**A**: When GDScript awaits on a method, it actually awaits on the completed signal of the state object returned when awaiting. This class seems to not be exposed to the API, but can still be used, hence the following code should be valid:

```GDScript
func my_first_coroutine():
    await get_tree().process_frame
    return 42

func my_second_coroutine():
    var my_variable := Thread.suspend(my_first_coroutine().completed) as int
    print(my_variable) # Prints 42
```
